Main.sentence: English literature is a form of ___E:literature U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literature)___ written in the ___E:English language U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language)___ from the ___E:English-speaking world U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English-speaking_world)___ .
The English language has developed over more than 1,400 years.

The earliest forms of English, a set of ___E:Anglo-Frisian dialects U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Frisian_languages)___ brought to ___E:Great Britain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain)___ by ___E:Anglo-Saxon settlers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxon_settlement_of_Britain)___ in the fifth century, are called ___E:Old English U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_English)___ .
Beowulf is the most famous work in Old English.
Despite being set in ___E:Scandinavia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scandinavia)___ , it has achieved national epic status in England.

However, following the ___E:Norman Conquest U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Conquest)___ of England in 1066, the written form of the ___E:Anglo-Saxon language U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_English)___ became less common.
Under the influence of the new aristocracy, French became the standard language of courts, parliament, and polite society.
The English spoken after the Normans came is known as ___E:Middle English U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_English)___ .

This form of English lasted until the 1470s, when the ___E:Chancery Standard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancery_Standard)___ (late Middle English), a ___E:London U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London)___ -based form of English, became widespread. ___E:Geoffrey Chaucer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffrey_Chaucer)___ , author of The Canterbury Tales , was a significant figure developing the legitimacy of ___E:vernacular U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernacular)___ Middle English at a time when the dominant literary languages in England were still French and Latin.

The ___E:invention of the printing press U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movable_type)___ by ___E:Johannes Gutenberg U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Gutenberg)___ in 1439 also helped to standardise the language, as did the King James Bible (1611),  and the ___E:Great Vowel Shift U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Vowel_Shift)___ .

Poet and playwright ___E:William Shakespeare U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shakespeare)___ is widely regarded as the greatest writer in the English language and one of the world's greatest dramatists.
His plays have been translated into every primary ___E:living language U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_language)___ and are performed more often than those of any other playwright.
In the nineteenth century, Sir ___E:Walter Scott U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Scott)___ 's historical romances inspired a generation of European painters, composers, and writers.
The English language spread throughout the world with the development of the ___E:British Empire U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire)___ between the late 16th and early 18th centuries.
At its height, it was the ___E:largest empire in history U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_largest_empires)___ .

By 1913, the British Empire held sway over 412 million people, 23% of the world population at the time.  During the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, these colonies and ___E:the US started to produce U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_literature)___ their significant literary traditions in English.

Cumulatively, from 1907 to the present, writers from ___E:Great Britain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain)___ , ___E:Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_literature)___ , the US, and former British colonies have received the ___E:Nobel Prize in Literature U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature)___ for works in English: more than in any other language.

___E:Old English literature U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_English_literature)___ , or Anglo-Saxon literature, encompasses the surviving literature written in ___E:Old English U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_English)___ in ___E:Anglo-Saxon England U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxon_England)___ , in the period after the settlement of the ___E:Saxons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_people)___ and other Germanic tribes in England ( ___E:Jutes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jutes)___ and the ___E:Angles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angles_(tribe))___ ) c. 450, after the withdrawal of the ___E:Romans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Romans)___ , and "ending soon after the Norman Conquest" in 1066.  These works include genres such as ___E:epic poetry U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_poem)___ , ___E:hagiography U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagiography)___ , ___E:sermons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sermon)___ , ___E:Bible U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bible)___ translations, legal works, ___E:chronicles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chronicle)___ and riddles.
In all there are about 400 surviving ___E:manuscripts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuscript)___ from the period.

Widsith , which appears in the ___E:Exeter Book U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exeter_Book)___ of the late 10th century, gives a list of kings of tribes ordered according to their popularity and impact on history, with ___E:Attila U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attila)___ King of the ___E:Huns U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huns)___ coming first, followed by ___E:Eormanric U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ermanaric)___ of the ___E:Ostrogoths U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostrogoths)___ .  : 187 It may also be the oldest extant work that tells the ___E:Battle of the Goths and Huns U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hl%C3%B6%C3%B0skvi%C3%B0a)___ , which is also told in such later Scandinavian works as ___E:Hervarar's saga U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hervarar_saga_ok_Hei%C3%B0reks)___ and Gesta Danorum .  : 179 ___E:Lotte Hedeager U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lotte_Hedeager)___ argues that the work is far older, however, and that it likely dates back to the late 6th or early 7th century, citing the author's knowledge of historical details and accuracy as proof of its authenticity.  : 184–86 She does note, however, that some authors, such as ___E:John Niles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_D._Niles)___ , have argued the work was invented in the 10th century.  : 181–84

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle is a collection of ___E:annals U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annals)___ in ___E:Old English U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_English)___ , from the 9th century, that ___E:chronicles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chronicle)___ the history of the ___E:Anglo-Saxons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxons)___ .
The poem Battle of Maldon also deals with history.

This is a work of uncertain date, celebrating the ___E:Battle of Maldon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Maldon)___ of 991, at which the Anglo-Saxons failed to prevent a ___E:Viking U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viking)___ invasion.

___E:Oral tradition U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orature)___ was very strong in early ___E:English culture U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxon_England)___ and most literary works were written to be performed.   ___E:Epic poems U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_poetry)___ were very popular, and some, including Beowulf , have survived to the present day. Beowulf is the most famous work in Old English, and has achieved ___E:national epic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_epic)___ status in England, despite being set in Scandinavia.

The only surviving manuscript is the ___E:Nowell Codex U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nowell_Codex)___ , the precise date of which is debated, but most estimates place it close to the year 1000. Beowulf is the conventional title,  and its composition is dated between the 8th   and the early 11th century.

Nearly all Anglo-Saxon authors are anonymous: twelve are known by name from medieval sources, but only four of those are known by their vernacular works with any certainty: ___E:Cædmon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A6dmon)___ , ___E:Bede U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bede)___ , ___E:Alfred the Great U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_the_Great)___ , and ___E:Cynewulf U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cynewulf)___ .
Cædmon is the earliest English poet whose name is known,  [pages needed] and his only known surviving work Cædmon's Hymn probably dates from the late 7th century.

The poem is one of the earliest attested examples of Old English and is, with the ___E:runic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runic)___ ___E:Ruthwell Cross U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruthwell_Cross)___ and ___E:Franks Casket U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franks_Casket)___ inscriptions, one of three candidates for the earliest attested example of Old English poetry.
It is also one of the earliest recorded examples of sustained poetry in a ___E:Germanic language U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germanic_languages)___ .
The poem, The Dream of the Rood , was inscribed upon the ___E:Ruthwell Cross U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruthwell_Cross)___ .  [pages needed]
Two ___E:Old English U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_English)___ poems from the late 10th century are The Wanderer and The Seafarer .

Both have a religious theme, and Marsden describes The Seafarer as "an exhortatory and didactic poem, in which the miseries of winter seafaring are used as a metaphor for the challenge faced by the committed Christian".

Classical antiquity was not forgotten in Anglo-Saxon England, and several Old English poems are adaptations of ___E:late classical U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Antiquity)___ philosophical texts.

The longest is ___E:King Alfred U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred)___ 's 9th-century translation of ___E:Boethius U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boethius)___ ' Consolation of Philosophy .

In addition, the famous Ecclesiastical History of the English People ( ___E:Latin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_language)___ : Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum ), written by ___E:Bede U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bede)___ in Latin in about AD 731 was translated into Old English sometime between the end of the ninth century and about 930.

After the ___E:Norman Conquest U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Conquest)___ of England in 1066, the written form of the ___E:Anglo-Saxon language U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxon_language)___ became less common.
Under the influence of the new aristocracy, French became the standard language of courts, parliament, and polite society.

As the invaders integrated, their language and literature mingled with that of the natives, and the ___E:Norman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_language)___ dialects of the ruling classes became ___E:Anglo-Norman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Norman_language)___ .
From then until the 12th century, Anglo-Saxon underwent a gradual transition into ___E:Middle English U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_English)___ .

Political power was no longer in English hands, so that the West Saxon literary language had no more influence than any other dialect and Middle English literature was written in many dialects that corresponded to the region, history, culture, and background of individual writers.

In this period religious literature continued to enjoy popularity and ___E:Hagiographies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagiography)___ were written, adapted and translated: for example, The Life of Saint Audrey , by ___E:Eadmer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eadmer)___ .

During the writing of Ormulum ( c. 1150 – c. 1180 ),  the blending of both Old English and Anglo-Norman elements in English are highlighted for the first time, marking the beginning of the Middle English period.

Afterwards, ___E:Layamon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Layamon)___ in Brut adapted the ___E:Norman-French U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman-French)___ of ___E:Wace U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wace)___ to produce the first English-language work to present the legends of ___E:King Arthur U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Arthur)___ and the ___E:Knights of the Round Table U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knights_of_the_Round_Table)___ .
It was also the first historiography written in English since the ___E:Anglo-Saxon Chronicle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxon_Chronicle)___ .

___E:Middle English Bible translations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_English_Bible_translations)___ , notably ___E:Wycliffe's Bible U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wycliffe%27s_Bible)___ , helped to establish English as a literary language.

Wycliffe's Bible is the name now given to a group of ___E:Bible translations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bible_translations)___ into Middle English that were made under the direction of, or at the instigation of, ___E:John Wycliffe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wycliffe)___ .

They appeared between about 1382 and 1395.  These Bible translations were the chief inspiration and cause of the ___E:Lollard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lollard)___ movement, a pre- ___E:Reformation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformation)___ movement that rejected many of the teachings of the Roman ___E:Catholic Church U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church)___ .

Another literary genre, that of ___E:Romances U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romance_(heroic_literature))___ , appears in English from the 13th century, with King Horn and Havelock the Dane , based on Anglo-Norman originals such as the Romance of Horn (c. 1170),  but it was in the 14th century that major writers in English first appeared.

These were ___E:William Langland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langland)___ , ___E:Geoffrey Chaucer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffrey_Chaucer)___ and the so-called ___E:Pearl Poet U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_Poet)___ , whose most famous work is Sir Gawain and the Green Knight .

Langland's Piers Plowman (written c. 1360–1387) or Visio Willelmi de Petro Plowman ( William's Vision of Piers Plowman ) is a Middle English ___E:allegorical U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegorical)___ narrative poem, written in unrhymed ___E:alliterative verse U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliterative_verse)___ .
Sir Gawain and the Green Knight is a late 14th-century Middle English alliterative ___E:romance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chivalric_romance)___ .
It is one of the better-known Arthurian stories of an established type known as the "beheading game".
Developing from Welsh, Irish and English tradition, Sir Gawain highlights the importance of honour and chivalry.
Preserved in the same manuscript with Sir Gawayne were three other poems, now generally accepted as the work of the same author, including an intricate elegiac poem, Pearl .

The English dialect of these poems from the ___E:Midlands U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midlands_(England))___ is markedly different from that of the ___E:London U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London)___ -based Chaucer and, though influenced by French in the scenes at court in Sir Gawain , there are in the poems also many dialect words, often of Scandinavian origin, that belonged to northwest England.

Middle English lasted until the 1470s, when the ___E:Chancery Standard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancery_Standard)___ , a London-based form of English, became widespread and the printing press started to standardise the language.
Chaucer is best known today for The Canterbury Tales .

This is a collection of stories written in Middle English (mostly in ___E:verse U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verse_(poetry))___ although some are in ___E:prose U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prose)___ ), that are presented as part of a story-telling contest by a group of pilgrims as they travel together from ___E:Southwark U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwark)___ to the shrine of St ___E:Thomas Becket U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Becket)___ at ___E:Canterbury Cathedral U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_Cathedral)___ .

Chaucer is a significant figure in the development of the legitimacy of the ___E:vernacular U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernacular)___ , Middle English, at a time when the dominant literary languages in England were still French and Latin.

At this time, literature in England was being written in various languages, including Latin, Norman-French, and English: the multilingual nature of the audience for literature in the 14th century is illustrated by the example of ___E:John Gower U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Gower)___ .

A contemporary of ___E:William Langland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langland)___ and a personal friend of Chaucer, Gower is remembered primarily for three major works: the Mirroir de l'Omme , Vox Clamantis , and Confessio Amantis , three long poems written in ___E:Anglo-Norman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Norman_language)___ , Latin and Middle English respectively, which are united by common moral and political themes.

Significant religious works were also created in the 14th century, including those of ___E:Julian of Norwich U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_of_Norwich)___ and ___E:Richard Rolle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Rolle)___ .
Julian's Revelations of Divine Love (about 1393) is believed to be the first published book written by a woman in the English language.

A major work from the 15th century is Le Morte d'Arthur by Sir ___E:Thomas Malory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Malory)___ , which was printed by ___E:Caxton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Caxton)___ in 1485.  This is a compilation of some French and English Arthurian romances, and was among the earliest books printed in England.
It was popular and influential in the later revival of interest in the Arthurian legends.

In the ___E:Middle Ages U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages)___ , drama in the vernacular languages of Europe may have emerged from enactments of the ___E:liturgy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liturgy)___ . ___E:Mystery plays U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mystery_play)___ were presented in the porches of cathedrals or by strolling players on ___E:feast days U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calendar_of_saints)___ . ___E:Miracle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miracle_play)___ and mystery plays, along with ___E:morality plays U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morality_play)___ (or "interludes"), later evolved into more elaborate forms of drama, such as was seen on the Elizabethan stages.

Another form of medieval theatre was the ___E:mummers' plays U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mummers_Play)___ , a form of early street theatre associated with the ___E:Morris dance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_dance)___ , concentrating on themes such as ___E:Saint George U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_George)___ and the ___E:Dragon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_dragon)___ and ___E:Robin Hood U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood)___ .

These were ___E:folk tales U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folklore)___ re-telling old stories, and the actors travelled from town to town performing these for their audiences in return for money and hospitality.

Mystery plays and miracle plays are among the earliest formally developed ___E:plays U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Play_(theatre))___ in ___E:medieval Europe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_Europe)___ .

Medieval mystery plays focused on the representation of ___E:Bible U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bible)___ stories in ___E:churches U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_(building))___ as ___E:tableaux U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tableau_vivant)___ with accompanying ___E:antiphonal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiphon)___ song. They developed from the 10th to the 16th century, reaching the height of their popularity in the 15th century before being rendered obsolete by the rise of professional theatre.
There are four complete or nearly complete extant English biblical collections of plays from the late medieval period.
The most complete is the York cycle of 48 pageants.

They were performed in the city of ___E:York U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/York)___ , from the middle of the 14th century until 1569.  Besides the Middle English drama, there are three surviving plays in ___E:Cornish U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornish_language)___ known as the ___E:Ordinalia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinalia)___ .

Having grown out of the religiously based ___E:mystery plays U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mystery_play)___ of the Middle Ages, the ___E:morality play U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morality_play)___ is a ___E:genre U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genre)___ of medieval and ___E:early Tudor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tudor_period)___ theatrical entertainment, which represented a shift towards a more secular base for European theatre.

Morality plays are a type of ___E:allegory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegory)___ in which the ___E:protagonist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protagonist)___ is met by ___E:personifications U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personification)___ of various ___E:moral U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morality)___ attributes who try to prompt him to choose a godly life over one of evil. The plays were most popular in Europe during the 15th and 16th centuries.

The Somonyng of Everyman ( The Summoning of Everyman ) (c. 1509–1519), usually referred to simply as Everyman , is a late 15th-century English morality play. Like ___E:John Bunyan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bunyan)___ 's allegory Pilgrim's Progress (1678), Everyman examines the question of ___E:Christian salvation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_salvation)___ through the use of allegorical characters.

The ___E:English Renaissance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Renaissance)___ as a part of the ___E:Northern Renaissance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Renaissance)___ was a ___E:cultural U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_movement)___ and ___E:artistic movement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_movement)___ in England dating from the late 15th to the 17th century.
It is associated with the pan-European ___E:Renaissance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance)___ that is usually regarded as beginning in Italy in the late 14th century.
Like most of northern Europe, England saw little of these developments until more than a century later – Renaissance style and ideas were slow in penetrating England.

Many scholars see the beginnings of the English Renaissance during the reign of ___E:Henry VIII U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VIII)___  and the ___E:Elizabethan era U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabethan_era)___ in the second half of the 16th century is usually regarded as the height of the English Renaissance.
The influence of the Italian Renaissance can also be found in the poetry of ___E:Thomas Wyatt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Wyatt_(poet))___ , one of the earliest English Renaissance poets.

He was responsible for many innovations in English poetry, and alongside ___E:Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Howard,_Earl_of_Surrey)___ introduced the ___E:sonnet U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonnet)___ from Italy into England in the early 16th century.

After ___E:William Caxton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Caxton)___ introduced the printing press in England in 1476, ___E:vernacular literature U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernacular_literature)___ flourished.

The ___E:Reformation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Reformation)___ inspired the production of vernacular ___E:liturgy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liturgy)___ which led to the Book of Common Prayer (1549), a lasting influence on literary language.

___E:Edmund Spenser U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmund_Spenser)___ was one of the most important poets of the Elizabethan period, author of The Faerie Queene (1590 and 1596), an epic poem and fantastical ___E:allegory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegory)___ celebrating the ___E:Tudor dynasty U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tudor_dynasty)___ and ___E:Elizabeth I U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_I)___ .

Another major figure, ___E:Sir Philip Sidney U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Sidney)___ , was an English poet, whose works include Astrophel and Stella , The Defence of Poetry , and The Countess of Pembroke's Arcadia .

Poems intended to be set to music as songs, such as those by ___E:Thomas Campion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Campion)___ , became popular as printed literature was disseminated more widely in households. ___E:John Donne U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Donne)___ was another important figure in Elizabethan poetry (see Jacobean poetry below).

Among the earliest Elizabethan plays are Gorboduc (1561) by ___E:Sackville U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Sackville,_1st_Earl_of_Dorset)___ and ___E:Norton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Norton)___ , and ___E:Thomas Kyd U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Kyd)___ 's The Spanish Tragedy (1592).

Gorboduc is notable especially as the first ___E:verse drama U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verse_drama)___ in ___E:English U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language)___ to employ ___E:blank verse U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blank_verse)___ , and for the way it developed elements, from the earlier ___E:morality plays U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morality_play)___ and ___E:Senecan tragedy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senecan_tragedy)___ , in the direction which would be followed by later playwrights.

The Spanish Tragedy  is an Elizabethan ___E:tragedy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tragedy)___ written by ___E:Thomas Kyd U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Kyd)___ between 1582 and 1592, which was popular and influential in its time, and established a new ___E:genre U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genre)___ in English literature theatre, the ___E:revenge play U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revenge_play)___ .

___E:William Shakespeare U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shakespeare)___ stands out in this period as a ___E:poet U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poet)___ and ___E:playwright U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playwright)___ as yet unsurpassed.

Shakespeare wrote plays in a variety of genres, including ___E:histories U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakespearean_history)___ (such as Richard III and Henry IV ), ___E:tragedies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakespearean_tragedy)___ (such as Hamlet , Othello , and Macbeth ) ___E:comedies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakespearean_comedy)___ (such as Midsummer Night's Dream , As You Like It , and Twelfth Night ) and the late ___E:romances U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shakespeare%27s_late_romances)___ , or tragicomedies.
Shakespeare's career continues in the Jacobean period.

Other important figures in ___E:Elizabethan theatre U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabethan_theatre)___ include ___E:Christopher Marlowe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Marlowe)___ , and ___E:Ben Jonson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Jonson)___ , ___E:Thomas Dekker U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Dekker_(poet))___ , ___E:John Fletcher U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Fletcher_(playwright))___ and ___E:Francis Beaumont U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Beaumont)___ .

In the early 17th century ___E:Shakespeare U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shakespeare)___ wrote the so-called " ___E:problem plays U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakespearean_problem_play)___ ", as well as a number of his best known ___E:tragedies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakespearean_tragedy)___ , including Macbeth and King Lear .

In his final period, Shakespeare turned to ___E:romance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakespeare%27s_late_romances)___ or ___E:tragicomedy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tragicomedy)___ and completed three more major plays, including The Tempest .
Less bleak than the tragedies, these four plays are graver in tone than the comedies of the 1590s, but they end with reconciliation and the forgiveness of potentially tragic errors.

After Shakespeare's death, the poet and dramatist ___E:Ben Jonson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Jonson)___ was the leading literary figure of the ___E:Jacobean era U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobean_era)___ .
Jonson's aesthetics hark back to the Middle Ages and his characters embody the ___E:theory of humours U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humours)___ , which was based on contemporary medical theory.
Jonson's comedies include Volpone (1605 or 1606) and Bartholomew Fair (1614).

Others who followed Jonson's style include ___E:Beaumont and Fletcher U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaumont_and_Fletcher)___ , who wrote the popular comedy, The Knight of the Burning Pestle (probably 1607–1608), a satire of the rising middle class.

Another popular style of theatre during Jacobean times was the ___E:revenge play U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revenge_play)___ , which was popularized in the Elizabethan era by ___E:Thomas Kyd U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Kyd)___ , and then further developed later by ___E:John Webster U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Webster)___ , The White Devil (1612) and The Duchess of Malfi (1613).

Other revenge tragedies include The Changeling written by ___E:Thomas Middleton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Middleton)___ and ___E:William Rowley U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Rowley)___ .

___E:George Chapman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Chapman)___ is remembered chiefly for his famous translation in 1616 of ___E:Homer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homer)___ 's Iliad and Odyssey into English verse.
This was the first ever complete translations of either poem into the English language.

The translation had a profound influence on English literature and inspired ___E:John Keats U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Keats)___ 's famous sonnet "On First Looking into Chapman's Homer" (1816).

Shakespeare popularized the ___E:English sonnet U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_sonnet)___ , which made significant changes to ___E:Petrarch U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petrarch)___ 's model.

A collection of 154 by ___E:sonnets U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakespeare%27s_sonnets)___ , dealing with themes such as the passage of time, love, beauty and mortality, were first published in a 1609 quarto.

Besides Shakespeare and Ben Jonson, the major poets of the early 17th century included the ___E:Metaphysical poets U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metaphysical_poets)___ : ___E:John Donne U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Donne)___ , ___E:George Herbert U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Herbert)___ , ___E:Henry Vaughan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Vaughan)___ , ___E:Andrew Marvell U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Marvell)___ and ___E:Richard Crashaw U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Crashaw)___ .
Their style was characterized by ___E:wit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wit)___ and metaphysical conceits, that is, far-fetched or unusual similes or metaphors.
The most important prose work of the early 17th century was the ___E:King James Bible U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_James_Version)___ .

This, one of the most massive translation projects in the history of English up to this time, was started in 1604 and completed in 1611. This represents the culmination of a tradition of ___E:Bible translation into English U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bible_translations_into_English)___ that began with the work of ___E:William Tyndale U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Tyndale)___ , and it became the standard ___E:Bible U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bible)___ of the ___E:Church of England U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England)___ .

The ___E:Metaphysical poets U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metaphysical_poets)___ ___E:John Donne U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Donne)___ and ___E:George Herbert U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Herbert)___ were still alive after 1625, and later in the 17th century a second generation of metaphysical poets were writing, including ___E:Richard Crashaw U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Crashaw)___ , ___E:Andrew Marvell U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Marvell)___ , ___E:Thomas Traherne U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Traherne)___ and ___E:Henry Vaughan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Vaughan)___ .

The Cavalier poets were another important group of 17th-century poets, who came from the classes that supported King Charles I during the English Civil War (1642–1651). (King Charles reigned from 1625 and was executed in 1649).

The best known of the ___E:Cavalier poets U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalier_poet)___ are ___E:Robert Herrick U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Herrick_(poet))___ , ___E:Richard Lovelace U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Lovelace_(poet))___ , ___E:Thomas Carew U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Carew)___ and ___E:Sir John Suckling U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Suckling_(poet))___ .
They "were not a formal group, but all were influenced by" Ben Jonson.
Most of the Cavalier poets were courtiers, with notable exceptions.

For example, Robert Herrick was not a courtier, but his style marks him as a Cavalier poet. Cavalier works make use of allegory and classical allusions, and are influenced by Roman authors Horace, ___E:Cicero U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cicero)___ and ___E:Ovid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ovid)___ . ___E:John Milton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Milton)___ "was the last great poet of the English Renaissance"  and published a number of works before 1660, including L'Allegro (1631), Il Penseroso (1634), the masque Comus (1638) and Lycidas (1638).
However, his major epic works, including Paradise Lost (1667) were published in the Restoration period.

Restoration literature includes both Paradise Lost and the ___E:Earl of Rochester U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wilmot,_2nd_Earl_of_Rochester)___ 's Sodom, the sexual comedy of The Country Wife and the moral wisdom of Pilgrim's Progress.

It saw Locke's Two Treatises on Government, the founding of the ___E:Royal Society U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Society)___ , the experiments and the holy meditations of ___E:Robert Boyle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Boyle)___ , the ___E:hysterical attacks on theatres U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_View_of_the_Immorality_and_Profaneness_of_the_English_Stage)___ from ___E:Jeremy Collier U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Collier)___ , the pioneering of literary criticism from Dryden, and the first newspapers.

The official break in literary culture caused by censorship and radically moralist standards under Cromwell's Puritan regime created a gap in literary tradition, allowing a seemingly fresh start for all forms of literature after the Restoration.

During the Interregnum, the royalist forces attached to the court of ___E:Charles I U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England)___ went into exile with the twenty-year-old ___E:Charles II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England)___ .
The nobility who travelled with Charles II were therefore lodged for over a decade in the midst of the continent's literary scene.
___E:John Milton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Milton)___ , one of the greatest English poets, wrote at this time of religious flux and political upheaval.
Milton is best known for his epic poem Paradise Lost (1667).

Milton's poetry and prose reflect deep personal convictions, a passion for freedom and self-determination, and the urgent issues and political turbulence of his day. His celebrated Areopagitica , written in condemnation of pre-publication censorship, is among history's most influential and impassioned defenses of ___E:free speech U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_speech)___ and ___E:freedom of the press U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_the_press#United_Kingdom)___ .
The largest and most important poetic form of the era was satire.
In general, publication of satire was done anonymously, as there were great dangers in being associated with a satire.

___E:John Dryden U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dryden)___ was an influential English poet, literary critic, translator, and playwright who dominated the literary life of Restoration England to such a point that the period came to be known in literary circles as the "Age of Dryden".
He established the heroic couplet as a standard form of English poetry.

Dryden's greatest achievements were in satiric verse in works like the mock-heroic MacFlecknoe (1682).  ___E:Alexander Pope U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Pope)___ was heavily influenced by Dryden, and often borrowed from him; other writers in the 18th century were equally influenced by both Dryden and Pope.

Prose in the Restoration period is dominated by ___E:Christian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity)___ religious writing, but the Restoration also saw the beginnings of two genres that would dominate later periods, fiction and journalism.
Religious writing often strayed into political and economic writing, just as political and economic writing implied or directly addressed religion.
The Restoration was also the time when ___E:John Locke U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Locke)___ wrote many of his philosophical works.
His two Treatises on Government, which later inspired the thinkers in the ___E:American Revolution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolution)___ .
The Restoration moderated most of the more strident sectarian writing, but radicalism persisted after the Restoration.

Puritan authors such as ___E:John Milton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Milton)___ were forced to retire from public life or adapt, and those authors who had preached against monarchy and who had participated directly in the ___E:regicide U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regicide)___ of ___E:Charles I U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England)___ were partially suppressed.

Consequently, violent writings were forced underground, and many of those who had served in the Interregnum attenuated their positions in the Restoration. ___E:John Bunyan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bunyan)___ stands out beyond other religious authors of the period.
Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress is an ___E:allegory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegory)___ of personal salvation and a guide to the Christian life.
During the Restoration period, the most common manner of getting news would have been a ___E:broadsheet U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadsheet)___ publication.
A single, large sheet of paper might have a written, usually partisan, account of an event.
It is impossible to satisfactorily date the beginning of the novel in English.
However, long fiction and fictional biographies began to distinguish themselves from other forms in England during the Restoration period.
An existing tradition of Romance fiction in France and Spain was popular in England.

One of the most significant figures in the rise of the novel in the Restoration period is ___E:Aphra Behn U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aphra_Behn)___ , author of Oroonoko (1688), who was not only the first professional female novelist, but she may be among the first professional novelists of either sex in England.
As soon as the previous Puritan regime's ban on public stage representations was lifted, ___E:drama U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drama)___ recreated itself quickly and abundantly.

The most famous plays of the early Restoration period are the unsentimental or "hard" comedies of ___E:John Dryden U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dryden)___ , ___E:William Wycherley U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Wycherley)___ , and ___E:George Etherege U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Etherege)___ , which reflect the atmosphere at Court, and celebrate an aristocratic ___E:macho U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machismo)___ lifestyle of unremitting sexual intrigue and conquest.
After a sharp drop in both quality and quantity in the 1680s, the mid-1690s saw a brief second flowering of the drama, especially comedy.

Comedies like ___E:William Congreve U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Congreve_(playwright))___ 's The Way of the World (1700), and ___E:John Vanbrugh U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Vanbrugh)___ 's The Relapse (1696) and The Provoked Wife (1697) were "softer" and more middle-class in ethos, very different from the aristocratic ___E:extravaganza U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extravaganza)___ twenty years earlier, and aimed at a wider audience.

During the 18th century literature reflected the worldview of the ___E:Age of Enlightenment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Enlightenment)___ (or Age of Reason): a rational and scientific approach to religious, social, political, and economic issues that promoted a secular view of the world and a general sense of progress and perfectibility.

Led by the philosophers who were inspired by the discoveries of the previous century by people like ___E:Isaac Newton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Newton)___ and the writings of ___E:Descartes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Descartes)___ , ___E:John Locke U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Locke)___ and ___E:Francis Bacon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Bacon)___ .
They sought to discover and to act upon universally valid principles governing humanity, nature, and society.
They variously attacked spiritual and scientific authority, dogmatism, intolerance, censorship, and economic and social restraints.
They considered the state the proper and rational instrument of progress.
The extreme rationalism and skepticism of the age led naturally to deism and also played a part in bringing the later reaction of ___E:romanticism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanticism)___ .
The Encyclopédie of Denis Diderot epitomized the spirit of the age.

The term Augustan literature derives from authors of the 1720s and 1730s themselves, who responded to a term that ___E:George I of Great Britain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_I_of_Great_Britain)___ preferred for himself.

While George I meant the title to reflect his might, they instead saw in it a reflection of ___E:Ancient Rome U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Rome)___ 's transition from rough and ready literature to highly political and highly polished literature.

It is an age of exuberance and scandal, of enormous energy and inventiveness and outrage, that reflected an era when English, Welsh, Scottish, and Irish people found themselves in the midst of an expanding economy, lowering barriers to education, and the beginnings of the ___E:Industrial Revolution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_Revolution)___ .

It was during this time that the poet ___E:James Thomson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Thomson_(poet,_born_1700))___ produced his melancholy The Seasons (1728–1730) and ___E:Edward Young U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Young)___ wrote his poem Night Thoughts (1742), though the most outstanding poet of the age is ___E:Alexander Pope U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Pope)___ (1688–1744).
It is also the era that saw a serious competition over the proper model for the ___E:pastoral U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pastoral_poetry)___ .
In criticism, poets struggled with a doctrine of decorum, of matching proper words with proper sense and of achieving a diction that matched the gravity of a subject.

At the same time, the ___E:mock-heroic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mock-heroic)___ was at its zenith and Pope's Rape of the Lock (1712–1717) and The Dunciad (1728–1743) are still considered to be the greatest mock-heroic poems ever written.
Pope also translated the Iliad (1715–1720) and the Odyssey (1725–1726).
Since his death, Pope has been in a constant state of re-evaluation.

Drama in the early part of the period featured the last plays of ___E:John Vanbrugh U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Vanbrugh)___ and ___E:William Congreve U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Congreve_(playwright))___ , both of whom carried on the Restoration comedy with some alterations.

However, the majority of stagings were of lower ___E:farces U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farce)___ and much more serious and domestic tragedies. ___E:George Lillo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Lillo)___ and ___E:Richard Steele U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Steele)___ both produced highly moral forms of tragedy, where the characters and the concerns of the characters were wholly middle class or working class.
This reflected a marked change in the audience for plays, as royal patronage was no longer the important part of theatrical success.

Additionally, ___E:Colley Cibber U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colley_Cibber)___ and ___E:John Rich U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Rich_(producer))___ began to battle each other for greater and greater spectacles to present on stage.
The figure of ___E:Harlequin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlequin)___ was introduced, and ___E:pantomime U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantomime)___ theatre began to be staged.

This "low" comedy was quite popular, and the plays became tertiary to the staging. ___E:Opera U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opera)___ also began to be popular in London, and there was significant literary resistance to this Italian incursion.
In 1728 John Gay returned to the playhouse with The Beggar's Opera .
The ___E:Licensing Act 1737 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Licensing_Act_1737)___ brought an abrupt halt to much of the period's drama, as the theatres were once again brought under state control.

In prose, the earlier part of the period was overshadowed by the development of the English essay. ___E:Joseph Addison U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Addison)___ and ___E:Richard Steele U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Steele)___ 's The Spectator established the form of the British periodical essay.

However, this was also the time when the English ___E:novel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novel)___ was first emerging. ___E:Daniel Defoe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Defoe)___ turned from ___E:journalism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journalism)___ and writing criminal lives for the press to writing fictional criminal lives with Roxana and Moll Flanders.
He also wrote Robinson Crusoe (1719).
If Addison and Steele were dominant in one type of prose, then ___E:Jonathan Swift U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Swift)___ author of the satire Gulliver's Travels was in another.
In A Modest Proposal and the Drapier Letters , Swift reluctantly defended the Irish people from the predations of ___E:colonialism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonialism)___ .
This provoked riots and arrests, but Swift, who had no love of Irish ___E:Roman Catholics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church)___ , was outraged by the abuses he saw.

An effect of the ___E:Licensing Act 1737 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Licensing_Act_1737)___ was to cause more than one aspiring playwright to switch over to writing novels. ___E:Henry Fielding U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Fielding)___ began to write prose satire and novels after his plays could not pass the censors.

In the interim, ___E:Samuel Richardson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Richardson)___ had produced Pamela, or Virtue Rewarded (1740), and Henry Fielding attacked, what he saw, as the absurdity of this novel in, Joseph Andrews (1742) and Shamela (1741).

Subsequently, Fielding satirised Richardson's Clarissa (1748) with Tom Jones (1749). ___E:Tobias Smollett U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tobias_Smollett)___ (1721–1771) elevated the ___E:picaresque novel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picaresque_novel)___ with works such as Roderick Random (1748) and Peregrine Pickle (1751).

This period is known as the Age of Sensibility , but it is also sometimes described as the "Age of Johnson".  ___E:Samuel Johnson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Johnson)___ , often referred to as Dr Johnson, was an English author who made lasting contributions to English literature as a poet, essayist, moralist, literary critic, biographer, editor and ___E:lexicographer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lexicographer)___ .
Johnson has been described as "arguably the most distinguished man of letters in English history".

After nine years of work, Johnson's A Dictionary of the English Language was published in 1755, and it had a far-reaching effect on ___E:Modern English U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_English)___ and has been described as "one of the greatest single achievements of scholarship."

The second half of the 18th century saw the emergence of three major Irish authors: ___E:Oliver Goldsmith U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Goldsmith)___ , ___E:Richard Brinsley Sheridan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Brinsley_Sheridan)___ and ___E:Laurence Sterne U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurence_Sterne)___ .
Goldsmith is the author of The Vicar of Wakefield (1766), a pastoral poem The Deserted Village (1770) and two plays, The Good-Natur'd Man (1768) and She Stoops to Conquer (1773).
Sheridan's first play, The Rivals (1775), was performed at ___E:Covent Garden U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covent_Garden)___ and was an instant success.
He went on to become the most significant London playwright of the late 18th century with a play like The School for Scandal .

Both Goldsmith and Sheridan reacted against the sentimental comedy of the 18th-century theatre, writing plays closer to the style of ___E:Restoration comedy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Restoration_comedy)___ .

Sterne published his famous novel Tristram Shandy in parts between 1759 and 1767.  In 1778, ___E:Frances Burney U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frances_Burney)___ wrote Evelina , one of the first ___E:novels of manners U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novel_of_manners)___ .
Fanny Burney's novels "were enjoyed and admired by Jane Austen".

The Romantic movement in English literature of the early 19th century has its roots in 18th-century poetry, the ___E:Gothic novel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_novel)___ and the novel of sensibility.
This includes the ___E:graveyard poets U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graveyard_poets)___ , from the 1740s and later, whose works are characterised by gloomy meditations on mortality.

To this was added, by later practitioners, a feeling for the ___E:'sublime' U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sublime_(philosophy))___ and uncanny, and an interest in ancient English poetic forms and folk poetry.

The poets include ___E:Thomas Gray U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Gray)___ , Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard (1751) in  and ___E:Edward Young U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Young)___ , The Complaint, or Night Thoughts on Life, Death and Immortality (1742–1745).
Other precursors are ___E:James Thomson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Thomson_(poet,_born_1700))___ and ___E:James Macpherson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Macpherson)___ .

James Macpherson was the first Scottish poet to gain an international reputation, with his claim to have found poetry written by the ancient bard ___E:Ossian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ossian)___ .
The ___E:sentimental novel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentimental_novel)___ or "novel of sensibility" is a genre which developed during the second half of the 18th century.

It celebrates the emotional and intellectual concepts of sentiment, ___E:sentimentalism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentimentalism_(literature))___ , and ___E:sensibility U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sensibility)___ .

Sentimentalism, which is to be distinguished from sensibility, was a fashion in both poetry and prose fiction which began in the 18th century in reaction to the rationalism of the ___E:Augustan Age U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustan_literature)___ .

Among the most famous sentimental novels in English are ___E:Samuel Richardson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Richardson)___ 's Pamela, or Virtue Rewarded (1740), ___E:Oliver Goldsmith U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Goldsmith)___ 's Vicar of Wakefield (1766), ___E:Laurence Sterne U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurence_Sterne)___ 's Tristram Shandy (1759–67), and ___E:Henry Mackenzie U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Mackenzie)___ 's The Man of Feeling (1771).

Significant foreign influences were the Germans ___E:Goethe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goethe)___ , ___E:Schiller U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schiller)___ and ___E:August Wilhelm Schlegel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/August_Wilhelm_Schlegel)___ and French philosopher and writer ___E:Jean-Jacques Rousseau U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Jacques_Rousseau)___ .  ___E:Edmund Burke U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmund_Burke)___ 's A Philosophical Enquiry into the Origin of Our Ideas of the Sublime and Beautiful (1757) is another important influence.

The changing landscape, brought about by the ___E:Industrial Revolution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_Revolution)___ and ___E:British Agricultural Revolution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Agricultural_Revolution)___ , was another influence on the growth of the Romantic movement in Britain.

In the late 18th century, ___E:Horace Walpole U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Walpole)___ 's 1764 novel The Castle of Otranto created the ___E:Gothic fiction U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_fiction)___ genre, that combines elements of ___E:horror U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horror_fiction)___ and ___E:romance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romance_(heroic_literature))___ .  ___E:Ann Radcliffe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ann_Radcliffe)___ introduced the brooding figure of the gothic ___E:villain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Villain)___ which developed into the ___E:Byronic hero U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byronic_hero)___ .
Her The Mysteries of Udolpho (1795) is frequently cited as the archetypal Gothic novel.
A later generation of Gothic writing emerged with ___E:Mary Shelley U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Shelley)___ , remembered as the author of Frankenstein (1818).

The successful ___E:War of Independence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolution)___ led by colonists in British North America from 1775 to 1783, resulted in the formation of the ___E:United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States)___ .

This consequently led to the divergence of English letters in what became the United States from the mainstream of English literature, resulting in the development of a new American literature that sought to distinguish itself as part of the formation of a new American social and cultural identity.
This was the first English-language literature to develop outside of the British Isles.

The late colonial period already saw the publication of important prose tracts reflecting the political debates that culminated in the American revolution, written by important luminaries such as ___E:Samuel Adams U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Adams)___ , ___E:Josiah Quincy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josiah_Quincy_II)___ , ___E:John Dickinson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dickinson_(delegate))___ , and ___E:Joseph Galloway U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Galloway)___ , the last being a loyalist to the crown.
Two key figures were ___E:Benjamin Franklin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Franklin)___ and ___E:Thomas Paine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Paine)___ .
Franklin's Poor Richard's Almanack and The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin are esteemed works with their wit and influence toward the formation of a budding American identity.
