During the ___E:Revolutionary War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War)___ , poems and songs such as " ___E:Nathan Hale U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_Hale)___ " were popular.

Major satirists included ___E:John Trumbull U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Trumbull_(poet))___ and ___E:Francis Hopkinson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Hopkinson)___ . ___E:Philip Morin Freneau U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Morin_Freneau)___ also wrote poems about the War.

In the post-war period, ___E:Thomas Jefferson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson)___ established his place in American literature through his authorship of the ___E:Declaration of Independence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Declaration_of_Independence)___ , his influence on the ___E:U.S. Constitution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Constitution)___ , his autobiography, his Notes on the State of Virginia , and his many letters. ___E:The Federalist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Federalist)___ essays by ___E:Alexander Hamilton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Hamilton)___ , ___E:James Madison U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Madison)___ , and ___E:John Jay U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Jay)___ presented a significant historical discussion of American government organization and republican values. ___E:Fisher Ames U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisher_Ames)___ , ___E:James Otis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Otis,_Jr.)___ , and ___E:Patrick Henry U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Henry)___ are also valued for their political writings and orations.
Early American literature struggled to find a unique voice in existing literary genre, and this tendency was reflected in novels.
European styles were frequently imitated, but critics usually considered the imitations inferior.
In the late 18th and early 19th centuries, the first American novels were published.
These fictions were too lengthy to be printed for public reading.
Publishers took a chance on these works in hopes they would become steady sellers and need to be reprinted.

This scheme was ultimately successful because male and female literacy rates were increasing at the time. Among the first American novels are ___E:Thomas Attwood Digges U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Thomas_Attwood_Digges&action=edit&redlink=1)___ 's Adventures of Alonso , published in London in 1775 and ___E:William Hill Brown U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Hill_Brown)___ 's The Power of Sympathy published in 1789. Brown's novel depicts a tragic love story between siblings who fell in love without knowing they were related.
Also of note were important women writers such as ___E:Susanna Rowson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susanna_Rowson)___ who wrote Charlotte: A Tale of Truth (later re-issued as Charlotte Temple ).

Charlotte Temple is a seduction tale influenced by the novels of English writer ___E:Samuel Richardson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Richardson)___ , written in the third person, which warns against listening to the voice of love and counsels resistance.
She also wrote nine novels, six theatrical works, two collections of poetry, six textbooks, and countless songs.
Reaching more than a million and a half readers over a century and a half, Charlotte Temple was the biggest seller of the 19th century before Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin .

Another important writer was ___E:Hannah Webster Foster U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannah_Webster_Foster)___ , who wrote the popular The Coquette: Or, the History of Eliza Wharton , published in 1797.  The story about a woman who is seduced and later abandoned, The Coquette has been praised for its demonstration of the era's contradictory ideas of womanhood.  even as it has been criticized for delegitimizing protest against women's subordination.

Other important early American writers include ___E:Charles Brockden Brown U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Brockden_Brown)___ , ___E:William Gilmore Simms U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Gilmore_Simms)___ , ___E:Lydia Maria Child U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydia_Maria_Child)___ , and ___E:John Neal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Neal)___ .
___E:Romanticism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanticism)___ was an artistic, literary, and intellectual movement that originated in Europe toward the end of the 18th century.
Romanticism arrived later in other parts of the English-speaking world.

The Romantic period was one of major social change in England and Wales, because of the depopulation of the countryside and the rapid development of overcrowded industrial cities, that took place in the period roughly between 1750 and 1850. The movement of so many people in England was the result of two forces: the ___E:Agricultural Revolution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Agricultural_Revolution)___ , that involved the ___E:Enclosure U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enclosure)___ of the land, drove workers off the land, and the ___E:Industrial Revolution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_Revolution)___ which provided them employment.

Romanticism may be seen in part as a reaction to the Industrial Revolution,  though it was also a revolt against aristocratic social and political norms of the ___E:Age of Enlightenment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Enlightenment)___ , as well a reaction against the scientific ___E:rationalization U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rationalization_(sociology))___ of nature.
The ___E:French Revolution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Revolution)___ was an especially important influence on the political thinking of many of the Romantic poets.
The landscape is often prominent in the poetry of this period, so much so that the Romantics, especially perhaps Wordsworth, are often described as 'nature poets'.
However, the longer Romantic 'nature poems' have a wider concern because they are usually meditations on "an emotional problem or personal crisis".
___E:Robert Burns U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Burns)___ was a pioneer of the Romantic movement, and after his death he became a cultural icon in Scotland.
The poet, painter, and printmaker ___E:William Blake U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Blake)___ was another of the early Romantic poets.

Though Blake was generally unrecognised during his lifetime, he is now considered a seminal figure in the history of both the poetry and visual arts of the ___E:Romantic Age U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanticism)___ .

Among his most important works are Songs of Innocence (1789) and Songs of Experience (1794) "and profound and difficult 'prophecies' ", such as "Jerusalem: the Emanation of the Giant Albion" (1804–c.1820).

After Blake, among the earliest Romantics were the ___E:Lake Poets U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Poets)___ , including ___E:William Wordsworth U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Wordsworth)___ , ___E:Samuel Taylor Coleridge U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Taylor_Coleridge)___ , ___E:Robert Southey U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Southey)___ and journalist ___E:Thomas de Quincey U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_de_Quincey)___ .
However, at the time ___E:Walter Scott U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Scott)___ was the most famous poet.
In 1784, with Elegiac Sonnets , ___E:Charlotte Smith U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte_Smith_(writer))___ reintroduced the sonnet to English literature. [citation needed]

The early ___E:Romantic Poets U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romantic_poetry)___ brought a new emotionalism and introspection, and their emergence is marked by the first romantic manifesto in English literature, the "Preface" to Lyrical Ballads (1798).
The poems in Lyrical Ballads were mostly by Wordsworth, though Coleridge contributed " ___E:Rime of the Ancient Mariner U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rime_of_the_Ancient_Mariner)___ ".

Among Wordsworth's most important poems are " ___E:Lines Composed a Few Miles Above Tintern Abbey U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lines_Composed_a_Few_Miles_Above_Tintern_Abbey)___ ", " ___E:Resolution and Independence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resolution_and_Independence)___ ", " ___E:Ode: Intimations of Immortality from Recollections of Early Childhood U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ode:_Intimations_of_Immortality_from_Recollections_of_Early_Childhood)___ " and the autobiographical epic The Prelude .

___E:Robert Southey U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Southey)___ was another of the so-called " ___E:Lake Poets U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Poets)___ ", and ___E:Poet Laureate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poet_Laureate)___ for 30 years, although his fame has been long eclipsed by ___E:William Wordsworth U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Wordsworth)___ and ___E:Samuel Taylor Coleridge U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Taylor_Coleridge)___ . ___E:Thomas De Quincey U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_De_Quincey)___ is best known for his Confessions of an English Opium-Eater (1821).

Essayist ___E:William Hazlitt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Hazlitt)___ (1778–1830), friend of both Coleridge and Wordsworth, is best known today for his literary criticism, especially Characters of Shakespeare's Plays (1817–1818).

The second generation of Romantic poets includes ___E:Lord Byron U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Byron)___ , ___E:Percy Bysshe Shelley U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percy_Bysshe_Shelley)___ , ___E:Felicia Hemans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felicia_Hemans)___ and ___E:John Keats U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Keats)___ .

Byron, however, was still influenced by 18th-century satirists and was, perhaps the least 'romantic' of the three, preferring "the brilliant wit of ___E:Pope U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Pope)___ to what he called the 'wrong poetical system' of his Romantic contemporaries".
Byron achieved enormous fame and influence throughout Europe and ___E:Goethe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goethe)___ called Byron "undoubtedly the greatest genius of our century".
Shelley is perhaps best known for Ode to the West Wind , To a Skylark , and Adonais , an elegy written on the death of Keats.

His close circle of admirers included the most progressive thinkers of the day. A work like Queen Mab (1813) reveals Shelley "as the direct heir to the French and British revolutionary intellectuals of the 1790s".

Shelley became an idol of the next three or four generations of poets, including important ___E:Victorian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorian_era)___ and ___E:Pre-Raphaelite U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Raphaelite)___ poets such as ___E:Robert Browning U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Browning)___ , and ___E:Dante Gabriel Rossetti U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dante_Gabriel_Rossetti)___ , as well as later ___E:W. B. Yeats U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._B._Yeats)___ .

Though John Keats shared Byron and Shelley's radical politics, "his best poetry is not political",  but is especially noted for its sensuous music and imagery, along with a concern with material beauty and the transience of life.  Among his most famous works are " ___E:Ode to a Nightingale U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ode_to_a_Nightingale)___ ", " ___E:Ode on a Grecian Urn U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ode_on_a_Grecian_Urn)___ ", and " ___E:To Autumn U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/To_Autumn)___ ".
Keats has always been regarded as a major Romantic, "and his stature as a poet has grown steadily through all changes of fashion".

Although sticking to its forms, ___E:Felicia Hemans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felicia_Hemans)___ began a process of undermining the Romantic tradition, a deconstruction that was continued by ___E:Letitia Elizabeth Landon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letitia_Elizabeth_Landon)___ , as "an urban poet deeply attentive to themes of decay and decomposition".

Landon's novel forms of metrical romance and ___E:dramatic monologue U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dramatic_monologue)___ were much copied and contributed to her long-lasting influence on Victorian poetry.

Another important poet in this period was ___E:John Clare U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Clare)___ , the son of a farm labourer, who came to be known for his celebratory representations of the English countryside and his lamentation for the changes taking place in rural England.
His poetry has undergone a major re-evaluation and he is often now considered to be among the most important 19th-century poets.

___E:George Crabbe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Crabbe)___ was an English poet who, during the Romantic period, wrote "closely observed, realistic portraits of rural life ... in the ___E:heroic couplets U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heroic_couplet)___ of the ___E:Augustan age U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustan_literature#Poetry)___ ".
Modern critic Frank Whitehead has said that "Crabbe, in his verse tales in particular, is an important—indeed, a major—poet whose work has been and still is seriously undervalued."

One of the most popular novelists of the era was Sir ___E:Walter Scott U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Scott)___ , whose ___E:historical romances U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_romance)___ inspired a generation of painters, composers, and writers throughout Europe.
Scott's novel-writing career was launched in 1814 with Waverley , often called the first ___E:historical novel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_novel)___ .

The works of ___E:Jane Austen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Austen)___ critique the ___E:novels of sensibility U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentimental_novel)___ of the second half of the 18th century and are part of the transition to 19th-century realism.
Her plots in novels such as Pride and Prejudice (1813) and Emma (1815), though fundamentally comic, highlight the dependence of women on marriage to secure social standing and economic security.
The European Romantic movement reached America in the early 19th century.
American Romanticism was just as multifaceted and individualistic as it was in Europe.

Like the Europeans, the American Romantics demonstrated a high level of moral enthusiasm, commitment to individualism and the unfolding of the self, an emphasis on intuitive perception, and the assumption that the natural world was inherently good, while human society was corrupt.

Romantic ___E:Gothic literature U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_literature)___ made an early appearance with ___E:Washington Irving U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Irving)___ 's The Legend of Sleepy Hollow (1820) and Rip Van Winkle (1819), There are picturesque "local color" elements in Washington Irving's essays and especially his travel books.

From 1823 the prolific and popular novelist ___E:James Fenimore Cooper U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Fenimore_Cooper)___ began publishing his ___E:historical romances U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_romance)___ of frontier and Indian life. However, ___E:Edgar Allan Poe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Allan_Poe)___ 's tales of the macabre that first appeared in the early 1830s, and his poetry were more influential in France than at home.

During these years, sage writing developed as a new literary genre in which the author sought "to express notions about the world, man's situation in it, and how he should live."  John Holloway identified ___E:Benjamin Disraeli U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Disraeli)___ , ___E:George Eliot U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Eliot)___ , ___E:John Henry Newman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Henry_Newman)___ , and ___E:Thomas Hardy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Hardy)___ as writers of this type. Foremost among them was ___E:Thomas Carlyle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Carlyle)___ , a Scottish essayist, historian and philosopher who became "the undoubted head of English letters" in the 19th century.

Known as the Sage of ___E:Chelsea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea,_London)___ , the highly prolific author ___E:criticized the Industrial Revolution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Condition_of_England_question)___ ,  preached ___E:Hero-worship U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_man_theory)___ ,  and ___E:rebuked political economy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_dismal_science)___  in a series of works written in ___E:Carlylese U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlylese)___ , the name given to his unique style.

His influence on Victorian literature was nearly universal; in 1855, Eliot wrote that "there is hardly a superior or active mind of this generation that has not been modified by Carlyle's writings;" with the effect that if his books "were all burnt as the grandest of ___E:Suttees U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sati_(practice))___ on his funeral pile, it would be only like cutting down an oak after its acorns have sown a forest."
___E:John Ruskin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Ruskin)___ was an Anglo-Scottish art critic and philosopher who wrote in a similar vein, regarding Carlyle as his master.

The early part of his career was devoted to aesthetics, championing ___E:Turner U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._M._W._Turner)___ and the ___E:Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Raphaelite_Brotherhood)___ .

He later turned to ethics, expounding his ideas on educational reform and political economy, which were to have great influence on practices in England and throughout the world.   ___E:Matthew Arnold U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Arnold)___ was an English poet and critic who is also regarded as a sage writer, famous for his criticism of ___E:philistinism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philistinism)___ .

It was in the ___E:Victorian era U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorian_era)___ (1837–1901) that the novel became the leading ___E:literary genre U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_genre)___ in English.

Women played an important part in this rising popularity both as authors and as readers,  and monthly serialising of fiction also encouraged this surge in popularity, further upheavals which followed the ___E:Reform Act 1832 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_Act_1832)___ .

This was in many ways a reaction to rapid ___E:industrialization U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrialization)___ , and the social, political, and economic issues associated with it, and was a means of commenting on abuses of government and industry and the suffering of the poor, who were not profiting from England's economic prosperity.

Significant early examples of this genre include Sybil, or The Two Nations (1845) by ___E:Benjamin Disraeli U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Disraeli)___ , and ___E:Charles Kingsley U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Kingsley)___ 's Alton Locke (1849).

___E:Charles Dickens U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Dickens)___ emerged on the literary scene in the late 1830s and soon became probably the most famous novelist in the history of English literature.

Dickens fiercely satirised various aspects of society, including the ___E:workhouse U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Workhouse)___ in Oliver Twist , and the failures of the legal system in Bleak House .

An early rival to Dickens was ___E:William Makepeace Thackeray U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Makepeace_Thackeray)___ , who during the Victorian period ranked second only to him, but he is now known almost exclusively for Vanity Fair (1847).
The ___E:Brontë U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bront%C3%AB)___ sisters, Emily, Charlotte and Anne, were other significant novelists in the 1840s and 1850s.

Jane Eyre (1847), ___E:Charlotte Brontë U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte_Bront%C3%AB)___ 's most famous work, was the first of the sisters' novels to achieve success. ___E:Emily Brontë U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emily_Bront%C3%AB)___ 's novel was Wuthering Heights and, according to ___E:Juliet Gardiner U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juliet_Gardiner)___ , "the vivid sexual passion and power of its language and imagery impressed, bewildered and appalled reviewers,"  and led the Victorian public and many early reviewers to think that it had been written by a man.  The Tenant of Wildfell Hall (1848) by ___E:Anne Brontë U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_Bront%C3%AB)___ is now considered to be one of the first ___E:feminist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feminism)___ novels.

___E:Elizabeth Gaskell U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Gaskell)___ was also a successful writer and her North and South contrasts the lifestyle in the industrial north of England with the wealthier south.  ___E:Anthony Trollope U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Trollope)___ was one of the most successful, prolific and respected English novelists of the Victorian era. Trollope's novels portray the lives of the landowning and professional classes of early Victorian England.  ___E:George Eliot U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Eliot)___ , pen name of Mary Ann Evans, was a major novelist of the mid-Victorian period.

Her works, especially Middlemarch (1871–1872), are important examples of ___E:literary realism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_realism)___ , and are admired for their combination of high ___E:Victorian literary U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorian_literature)___ detail, with an intellectual breadth that removes them from the narrow geographic confines they often depict.

___E:George Meredith U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Meredith)___ is best remembered for his novels The Ordeal of Richard Feverel (1859), and The Egoist (1879). "His reputation stood very high well into" the 20th century but then seriously declined.

An interest in rural matters and the changing social and economic situation of the countryside is seen in the novels of ___E:Thomas Hardy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Hardy)___ (1840–1928), including The Mayor of Casterbridge (1886), and Tess of the d'Urbervilles (1891).

Hardy is a Victorian realist, in the tradition of ___E:George Eliot U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Eliot)___ ,  and like Charles Dickens he was also highly critical of much in Victorian society.

Another significant late-19th-century novelist is ___E:George Gissing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Gissing)___ (1857–1903), who published 23 novels between 1880 and 1903. His best known novel is New Grub Street (1891).

Although pre-dated by ___E:John Ruskin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Ruskin)___ 's The King of the Golden River in 1841, the history of the modern ___E:fantasy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fantasy_literature)___ genre is generally said to begin with ___E:George MacDonald U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_MacDonald)___ , the influential author of The Princess and the Goblin and Phantastes (1858).  ___E:William Morris U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Morris)___ wrote a series of ___E:romances U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chivalric_romance)___ in the 1880s and 1890s which are regarded as the first works of ___E:high fantasy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_fantasy)___ .

G. Wells U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._G._Wells)___ 's writing career began in the 1890s with ___E:science fiction U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction)___ novels like The Time Machine (1895), and The War of the Worlds (1898) which describes an invasion of late Victorian England by ___E:Martians U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martian)___ , and Wells is seen, along with Frenchman ___E:Jules Verne U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jules_Verne)___ , as a major figure in the development of the science fiction genre.

By the mid-19th century, the pre-eminence of literature from the British Isles began to be challenged by writers from the former American colonies.

A major influence on American writers at this time was ___E:Romanticism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanticism)___ , which gave rise to ___E:New England U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England)___ ___E:Transcendentalism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transcendentalism)___ , and the publication of ___E:Ralph Waldo Emerson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Waldo_Emerson)___ 's 1836 essay Nature is usually considered the watershed moment at which transcendentalism became a major cultural movement.

Thomas Carlyle had a strong influence on Emerson, transcendentalism,  and American writers generally, particularly his novel Sartor Resartus , of which the impact upon American literature has been described as "so vast, so pervasive, that it is difficult to overstate."

The romantic American novel developed fully with ___E:Nathaniel Hawthorne U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathaniel_Hawthorne)___ 's The Scarlet Letter (1850), a stark drama of a woman cast out of her community for committing adultery.
Hawthorne's fiction had a profound impact on his friend ___E:Herman Melville U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herman_Melville)___ .
In Moby-Dick (1851), an adventurous whaling voyage becomes the vehicle for examining such themes as obsession, the nature of evil, and human struggle against the elements.
By the 1880s, however, psychological and ___E:social realism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_realism)___ were competing with Romanticism in the novel.

American realist fiction has its beginnings in the 1870s with the works of ___E:Mark Twain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Twain)___ , ___E:William Dean Howells U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Dean_Howells)___ , and ___E:Henry James U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_James)___ .

Mark Twain (the pen name used by Samuel Langhorne Clemens) was the first major American writer to be born away from the East Coast—in the border state of ___E:Missouri U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri)___ .
His regional masterpieces were the novels Adventures of Tom Sawyer (1876) and Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884).
Twain's style changed the way Americans write their language.
His characters speak like real people and sound distinctively American, using local dialects, newly invented words, and regional accents.
___E:Henry James U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_James)___ was a major American novelist of the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
Although born in New York City, he spent most of his adult years in England.
Many of his novels center on Americans who live in or travel to Europe.
